nameStory: The Blood-winged Blister Beetle gets its dramatic name from two key features that make it memorable. Its wing covers (called elytra) are a striking reddish color that resembles dried blood, while 'blister beetle' refers to the family's ability to secrete a chemical that can cause painful blisters on human skin when handled.
description: The Blood-winged Blister Beetle is a medium-sized beetle with distinctive reddish wing covers that make it stand out among New England's insects. Like all blister beetles, it has a soft, somewhat cylindrical body that's quite different from the hard-shelled appearance of many beetles. These beetles are part of a fascinating family known for their chemical defenses and complex life cycles. Adults typically measure around half an inch in length and have a somewhat elongated appearance.

idTips.label: Reddish wing covers
idTips.description: The most striking feature - wing covers range from bright red to deep reddish-brown, giving them their 'blood-winged' name. The color is consistent across the entire wing surface.

idTips.label: Soft body texture
idTips.description: Unlike hard beetles like ground beetles, these feel somewhat soft and flexible when gently touched (though avoid direct contact due to blistering chemicals).

idTips.label: Cylindrical body shape
idTips.description: The body appears elongated and somewhat narrow, not round or heavily armored like many other beetle families.

idTips.label: Head and thorax coloring
idTips.description: The head and middle section are typically darker, often black or dark brown, creating a nice contrast with the red wing covers.

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are moderately long and clearly segmented, often held forward when the beetle is active.

habitat: Blood-winged Blister Beetles are found in open areas including meadows, fields, and forest edges throughout New England. They're often seen on flowering plants where they feed on pollen and nectar as adults. Look for them in sunny locations with abundant wildflowers, particularly in areas with sandy or well-drained soils.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but they're not commonly seen until the weather warms consistently.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible on flowers, particularly during warm, sunny days. This is the best time to spot them feeding on various wildflowers.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be active in early fall, but become less common as temperatures drop and flowers become scarce.
seasonality.winter: Not active - they overwinter in soil or under debris as larvae or pupae, completely hidden from view.

funFact: Blister beetles have one of the most bizarre life cycles in the insect world - their larvae are actually beneficial predators that hunt down grasshopper eggs underground, making them helpful pest controllers despite the adults' ability to blister human skin!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other red beetles like some ladybugs or cardinal beetles, but the Blood-winged Blister Beetle's soft, elongated body shape is quite different from the round, hard-shelled ladybugs. Remember: if it's red and soft-bodied, think blister beetle and avoid touching!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their intimidating name and chemical defenses, these beetles aren't aggressive and only release their blistering chemicals when threatened or crushed. The blistering agent, called cantharidin, was historically used in folk medicine but is quite dangerous - always observe these beautiful beetles from a respectful distance.
compareHints: The Blood-winged Blister Beetle is the only Tricrania species recorded in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other blister beetles in the region, it's distinguished by its consistent reddish wing covers - most other local blister beetles are black, metallic, or have striped patterns rather than the solid red coloration.
